items.prompt: Define the term 'location decision'.
items.canonical_answer: A location decision is the choice of the place, or geographical area, in which a business will set up and carry out its operations; a relocation decision is the same choice made again when a business that already operates decides to move.
marking_guidance: Precise meaning: the definition must name the choice of place or geographical area for setting up operations. Saying where a shop happens to stand is an example, not a definition.

items.prompt: A fish-canning factory in Walvis Bay sits beside the harbour where its catch is landed, while a hairdressing salon in Windhoek chose its site because the street outside is busy all day. Explain why the two businesses weigh location factors so differently.
items.canonical_answer: The reason is what each business needs from its site. The cannery main input is fresh fish, which is heavy and perishable, so being close to the harbour keeps transport short and the raw material fresh, and that matters far more to it than the number of passers-by. The salon sells a service straight to customers who must come to it, so its income depends on how many people pass and how easy the site is to reach; closeness to raw materials means nothing to a hairdresser. Because the two businesses draw their income from different things - transforming materials on site for one, reaching passing customers for the other - the factors they weigh differ in the same way.
marking_guidance: Reason: award for the purpose each business site serves - fresh materials for the cannery, passing customers for the salon - because the factor that matters is the one the business income depends on. Second reason: award for developing the contrast with the other side of the pair, showing why the factor that decides one does not decide the other.

items.prompt: Explain the features of the main location factors a manufacturing business weighs before choosing a site.
items.canonical_answer: The features of the set: closeness to raw materials and component suppliers, which shortens supply journeys and can lower transport costs; the skills and wages of local labour, which decide whether the business can recruit the people it needs; transport links such as roads, rail and ports, which move inputs in and finished goods out; the cost and dependability of the power supply machines rely on; room to expand if output rises; and government incentives, such as a subsidised site, that some areas offer to attract employers. What the set includes, taken together, is every running cost and constraint the site itself imposes on the business from the day it opens.
marking_guidance: Features: award for each element of the set - materials, labour skills and wages, transport links, energy, room to expand, incentives - up to the tariff, and for what the set includes overall: the costs and constraints the site itself imposes on the business.

items.prompt: A learner writes: 'The factors that decide where a factory locates also decide where a hairdressing salon locates.' Explain why this statement is wrong.
items.canonical_answer: The error is treating one set of factors as if every business shared it. In fact the two sets overlap only at the edges. A factory choice is dominated by closeness to materials, labour skills, transport links and energy, because its income depends on transforming inputs cheaply on site; a salon choice is dominated by closeness to customers and passing trade, because its income depends on people walking in. A factory in an industrial park beside a rail line may thrive where a salon would sit empty, and a salon on a busy street may thrive where a factory could not afford the rent or receive its lorries. The test that tells the two apart: ask whether the factor concerns the business inputs and running costs, which dominate a manufacturer choice, or reaching customers, which dominates a service choice.
marking_guidance: The error is named and corrected: in fact a manufacturer factors concern inputs and running costs, wrongly treated here as universal. Award the second part for the test that separates the confused pair - inputs and costs against closeness to customers.

items.prompt: A business that sells in several markets still has to pick one country to base its operations in. Define the term 'international location decision'.
items.canonical_answer: An international location decision is the choice of which country a business will set up and carry out its operations in; it weighs factors, such as political stability and the country laws, that barely differ between two towns in the same country.
marking_guidance: Precise meaning: the definition must name the choice of country for setting up operations, and may add that the factors it weighs extend beyond those a town-level choice involves.

items.prompt: Omaruru Juice Press bottles marula juice and sells nearly all of it in Namibia. It is deciding which country to build its new bottling plant in. In Namibia the plant would stand 40 km from its customers, wages would be N$6 800 a month and the rules are familiar. In a neighbouring country wages are N$4 300 a month and the government offers a five-year tax break, but the plant would stand 900 km from its customers, adding N$380 of transport per delivery lorry, and the unfamiliar legal system would take months to learn. Consider which country Omaruru Juice Press should locate its new plant in.
items.canonical_answer: Judgement: Omaruru Juice Press should keep the new plant in Namibia. The context that decides it: the juice is sold in Namibia, so the neighbouring-country site would add N$380 per lorry over 900 km - a transport cost that repeats for as long as the plant runs - while the wage saving of N$2 500 a month per worker is fixed and modest beside it. The criterion: what decides the choice is total recurring cost and risk for this business, not the most eye-catching single figure. The counterargument: a five-year tax break is a real gain, and monthly wages lower by N$2 500 is the other side of the case - if the business later exports across the border, the plant would already stand near that new market and the position could reverse. The condition the recommendation depends on: it holds provided sales stay concentrated in Namibia; if the business wins export orders across the border, the recommendation changes and the comparison would need recalculating.
marking_guidance: Judgement: award a clear recommendation between the two countries.
Context: award for using the facts of the business - the N$2 500 wage difference, the N$380 per lorry, the 900 km, the five-year tax break - not generalities.
Criterion: award for naming what decides it: recurring transport cost and risk against a fixed wage saving for this business.
Counterargument: award for the case against the recommendation - the tax break and export potential argue for the other side.
Condition: award for stating the recommendation depends on sales staying in Namibia; if the market shifts, the choice changes.

items.prompt: Panda Uniforms sews school shirts sold throughout Namibia. It is choosing which country to move its factory to. Country A has wages about a third lower than Namibia own and an expanding shirt market, but weak roads and a licensing system its managers do not know. Country B is next to Namibia with strong transport links, familiar rules and a small but stable market, at wages close to Namibia own. Explain which country Panda Uniforms should move to, using the factors that matter here.
items.canonical_answer: The context: Panda shirts are heavy, low-margin goods sold across Namibia, so delivery depends on good roads, and Country A weak transport links would slow every dispatch and could add cost per shirt for as long as the factory runs. The reasoning: Country A wage advantage is real, but a lower wage per month only helps if workers make similar output, and moving managers into an unfamiliar licensing system risks months of delay - both weaknesses of Country A here. The link to the choice: Country B keeps shirts moving to the Namibian market over familiar rules, and its near-Namibian wages remove most of Country A pull. Conclusion: Country B is the better choice for this business, because the factors that dominate its situation - transport to market and workable rules - both point there; Country A would suit a business selling mainly inside Country A own market.
marking_guidance: Context: award for using the named business facts - heavy low-margin shirts, wages, roads, licensing.
Reasoning: award for the link between each factor and what it does to the business costs or deliveries, with a because.
Conclusion: award a choice for this business that follows from the reasoning, with the reason it beats the alternative.

items.prompt: A shoe factory moves its production from Namibia to a country where wages are 40 per cent lower, expecting its costs to fall by the same 40 per cent. Explain how the move could lead to higher costs per shoe rather than lower ones.
items.canonical_answer: Condition: the starting point is a wage 40 per cent lower and the belief that cost per shoe falls with it. Mechanism: the cost of a shoe is built from the wage for the hours each shoe takes, plus materials and transport; if workers in the new country are less practised, each shoe takes more hours, so the wage saving can be used up by the extra hours, and the cost per shoe may not fall at all - it may rise. Consequence for the business: the cheaper production the business moved for does not appear, so prices cannot fall as planned, and the move has also added shipping distance to the market, weakening the business competitive position against rivals that stayed closer to their customers.
marking_guidance: Condition: award for tying the mechanism to the given starting point - the 40 per cent wage cut and the expectation built on it.
Mechanism: award for the why or how - cost per shoe is hours as well as wages, so productivity decides whether the saving survives.
Consequence: award for the effect on the business - no cost fall, plus added transport - and a second consequence for the business position against rivals.

items.prompt: Explain the elements a business should include in a comparison between two countries before locating operations in one of them.
items.canonical_answer: The elements to include: the cost and skill of labour, measured against output per worker rather than the wage alone; the size of the market in each country and the direction it is heading; closeness of each site to materials and to customers; the quality of transport links in each; the taxes each government charges and any incentives it offers; the legal system of each country and how strictly its rules are enforced; and political stability - how much a change of government could disrupt the business. What a sound comparison includes at the end is a weighing: the aim is not to count factors but to judge which of them matter most for the business doing the choosing, and to accept that the better country is the one whose strengths fit that business, not the one with the longest list.
marking_guidance: Elements: award one mark for each part included - labour cost and skill, market size, transport links, taxes and incentives, the legal system, political stability - and for what the comparison includes at the end: a weighing of which factors matter most for this business rather than a count.

items.prompt: A manager reads that monthly wages in Country K are N$3 900 against N$7 100 in Namibia, and concludes: 'Our cost per unit will be N$3 200 lower for every unit we make there.' Explain why the manager is mistaken.
items.canonical_answer: The mistake is reading a difference in monthly wages straight through to cost per unit. In fact, cost per unit depends on how many units each worker produces in a month, not on the wage alone: if a Namibian worker on N$7 100 makes 500 units a month while a Country K worker on N$3 900 makes 240, the wage cost per unit is higher in Country K, not lower - the N$3 200 monthly saving is spread over fewer units and runs out. The wage bill is also wrongly assumed here to be the whole of cost per unit: transport, materials and power may each cost more in Country K and reclaim the saving. The test that separates the pair: divide the monthly wage by the monthly output of a worker before claiming any unit-cost advantage.
marking_guidance: The mistake is named and corrected: in fact a wage comparison is wrongly read as a unit-cost comparison; award for the mechanism - output per worker decides the wage cost of a unit. Award the second part for the test that separates low wages from low unit costs: the wage divided by the output of a worker.

items.prompt: Define the term 'legal controls' as it applies to where a business may locate.

items.prompt: A town council zoning plan permits light industry solely on the estate north of the ring road, and a furniture workshop wants to open in a residential street. Explain how the control could lead the workshop to a different location, and what that change leads to for the business.
items.canonical_answer: Condition: the given starting point is a zoning plan that permits the workshop north of the ring road but not in the residential street it wanted. Mechanism: because opening in the street would break the plan, the council is likely to refuse permission or order the business out, so the practical choice the workshop actually holds is the estate - the site it wanted was not legally open to it. Consequence for the business: it must take the estate site, which may mean a longer journey for its customers and different rent, and this affects the stakeholder group that matters to a workshop - the people who buy fitted furniture and need to visit or be visited - so trade may dip until the business builds a reputation at the new address. The same control, though, protects the residents of the street from lorry noise, which is the objective the rule was written for.
marking_guidance: Condition: award for tying the chain to the starting point - the zoning plan rules out the residential street.
Mechanism: award for the why - permission would be refused, so the estate is the choice the business actually holds.
Consequence: award for the effect on the business and the stakeholder group - customers facing a longer journey, so trade may dip - and for the objective the rule serves: protecting residents.

items.prompt: Keetmanshoop Desert Devices assembles solar chargers. The council has granted planning permission for its new workshop on the edge of town, on condition that delivery lorries use the ring road and not the school street, and the area plan is due for review next year. Explain what these legal controls mean for the business and what it should do about them.
items.canonical_answer: The context: the business has its permission, but it comes with a condition - lorries must use the ring road - and with a date, next year review, when the condition could change. The reasoning: because breaking the condition could cost the business its permission, the ring-road route is part of the deal and should be planned into every dispatch, not treated as advice; and because the area plan is under review, a rule that suits the business today may be different tomorrow. The link to action: the business should record the condition in its operating procedures, brief its drivers, and check the review outcome before signing long delivery contracts. Conclusion: for this business the controls are workable provided it plans around them, and the right response is to build them into how it runs the site rather than to fight them.
marking_guidance: Context: award for using the named business facts - the ring-road condition and next year review.
Reasoning: award for the link between the condition and what happens if it is broken, and between the review and the risk of change.
Conclusion: award a choice for this business that follows the reasoning, such as planning routes around the condition and checking the review.

items.prompt: Explain the features of the role legal controls play in location decisions.
items.canonical_answer: The features of the role: legal controls set boundaries - they mark out where a business may and may not set up; they attach conditions, such as limits on noise, traffic or delivery hours, that a business must meet to keep its permission; they protect people and places, especially residents near industrial activity, which is the purpose behind most zoning; and they carry consequences, because a business that ignores them may face fines or an order to close. What the role includes overall is a narrowing of the business free choice: the business still chooses, but from the sites and on the terms the rules leave open.
marking_guidance: Features: award one mark for each element - boundaries, conditions, protection of residents, consequences for rule-breaking - and for what the role includes overall: a narrowed but not removed choice.

items.prompt: A learner writes: 'Legal controls and government incentives are two names for the same thing, since both come from the government and both affect where a business locates.' Explain the error in this statement.
items.canonical_answer: The error is confusing what pushes a business away from a site with what pulls it towards one. In fact the two work in opposite directions: a legal control restricts - it can forbid a site or load it with conditions the business must obey - while an incentive attracts, offering something, such as a tax break or a subsidised factory site, that makes a location more inviting. A zoning plan that blocks a business from a residential street is not a tax holiday. The test that tells them apart: ask whether the government action reduces the business options, which makes it a control, or adds to the appeal of an option, which makes it an incentive; a business may respond to both, but they are not one and the same thing.
marking_guidance: The error is named and corrected: in fact a control restricts and an incentive attracts - opposite directions, wrongly merged here. Award the second part for the test that separates the pair: fewer options against added appeal.

items.prompt: Define what it means to give a justified recommendation of a location for a business in given circumstances.
items.canonical_answer: To recommend and justify a location is to name the better site for the business in the circumstances given, and to support that choice with reasons drawn from those circumstances - showing why the factors that matter most for this business favour it.
marking_guidance: Precise meaning: the definition must include both parts - naming the better site and supporting it with reasons from the given circumstances. Naming a site alone is not a justification.

items.prompt: Etosha Stoneware makes hand-fired clay tableware, sold to tourists at its workshop shop and to gift shops across the region. Two sites are available for its new, larger workshop. Site A is on the outskirts of Otjiwarongo: rent is N$3 900 a month, clay suppliers are 20 minutes away, and tourists seldom pass. Site B is in the town centre beside the craft market: rent is N$7 400 a month, tourists pass all day, but clay deliveries would need a permit for heavy lorries in a restricted street. Consider which site Etosha Stoneware should choose.
items.canonical_answer: Judgement: Site B, the town-centre site, is the better choice for this business. The context: the business sells to tourists at its own workshop shop, and tourists pass Site B all day while Site A sees almost none, so the rent premium of N$3 500 a month buys the footfall its main sales channel depends on; clay deliveries at Site B are workable with a permit, which is a condition to arrange, while Site A is cheaper but buys a site its customers do not visit. The criterion: what decides this is not the cheapest rent but the site fit with how the business earns - direct sales to passing tourists. The counterargument: the other side is real - N$3 500 a month is a large gap for a small craft business, and the lorry permit adds a legal risk, so if sales were mainly wholesale to gift shops, Site A closeness to suppliers and lower rent would win instead. The condition: the recommendation holds provided tourists remain the main buyers at the workshop shop; if the balance shifts to wholesale, the choice changes to Site A.
marking_guidance: Judgement: award a clear recommendation between the two named sites.
Context: award for using the facts of the business - the N$3 900 and N$7 400 rents, tourist footfall, the lorry permit - not generalities.
Criterion: award for naming what decides it: fit with the business main sales channel, not the cheapest rent.
Counterargument: award for the case against the recommendation: the rent gap and the permit risk argue for Site A.
Condition: award for the recommendation depending on tourists remaining the main buyers; if wholesale dominates, the choice changes.

items.prompt: A new gym picks a cheap site on an industrial estate, expecting members to drive to it, because the rent is far below the shopping-centre site it rejected. Explain how this choice could lead to empty treadmills rather than healthy takings.

items.prompt: Explain the parts a well-justified location recommendation should include.
items.canonical_answer: The parts it should include: a clear choice of one site, named; the reasons for it, drawn from the circumstances of the business rather than from general praise of the site; a weighing of the factors that matter most for that business, because the right site follows from what the business sells and to whom; an acknowledgment of the alternative, showing why the rejected site is weaker for this business even though it has strengths; and the conditions the recommendation depends on, such as the market staying where it is. What it includes at bottom is an argument, not a description: the reader should be able to see not just which site was chosen but what would have to change for the other one to win.
marking_guidance: Parts: award one mark for each element - the named choice, reasons from the circumstances, the weighing, the rejected alternative, the conditions - and for what the recommendation includes overall: an argument rather than a description.

items.prompt: A student writes in a case answer: 'Site P has the lowest rent of all the sites, so the business should locate there.' Explain why this reasoning is flawed as a justification.
items.canonical_answer: The flaw is treating one cost figure as if it were the whole decision. In fact the most suitable site is the one whose features fit what the business sells and to whom: for a business that lives on passing trade, a cheap site no customer passes can be more expensive in lost sales than the rent saved, because rent is a monthly cost while a wrong site weakens income every day the business trades. A justification that names rent alone has not weighed the factors that matter most for this business and states no conditions. The test that tells a sound justification from this one: ask not which site is cheapest, but which site the business own circumstances point to - then check whether the reasoning shows that weighing.

items.prompt: The owner of Windhoek Coffee Roasters asks for advice before moving to bigger premises: it roasts beans at one site and runs three cafes. Write several linked points for the owner: state two factors that should drive the choice of the new roasting site, and two factors that should drive the choice for each new cafe, each with a reason, and close with what the owner should weigh most for each kind of site.
items.canonical_answer: Points for the roasting site: closeness to transport links, because sacks of green beans arrive and roasted batches leave in bulk, so easy access keeps delivery cost and freshness under control; and the wages and skills of local labour, because roasting and packing are skilled work and the site must be able to staff it. Points for a cafe: passing trade, because a cafe income depends on people who are already there deciding to come in; and rent that fits the sales the site can plausibly make, because a prime corner that out-earns its rent is worth more than a cheap street no one walks. What the owner should weigh: for the roastery the heaviest factors are inputs and distribution - a manufacturing-style choice; for each cafe the heaviest are customers and rent - a service-style choice; applying one test to both kinds of site would flatter the wrong one.
marking_guidance: Point: award for each point stated, up to two per kind of site.
Reason: award for the because behind each point - bulk access for roasting, footfall for cafes.
Context: award for applying each point to the named business two kinds of site, the roastery and each cafe, rather than in the abstract.

items.prompt: Rundu Rainwear makes waterproof jackets sold mainly in its home country. It plans a second factory and must choose between two countries. Country M: wages of N$4 200 a month, output of 180 jackets per worker a month, an eight-hour drive to the main market, and a five-year tax holiday for new factories. Country N: wages of N$6 600 a month, output of 320 jackets per worker a month, a one-hour drive to the main market, and standard taxes. Using the figures, consider which country Rundu Rainwear should build its factory in.
items.canonical_answer: Judgement: Rundu Rainwear should build in Country N. The criterion: what decides this is cost per jacket delivered to the market, not the monthly wage bill or any single headline figure. The counterargument: the five-year tax holiday is a real gain, and against a young business early losses it could shield the business while it establishes itself - the other side of the case, and the reason the decision is close at all. The condition: the recommendation for Country N holds provided output per worker stays as the figures state and the market stays at home; if either changes - productivity in Country M rises or the market shifts - the recommendation depends on recalculating the per-jacket comparison.

items.prompt: Plan, without writing the full answer, a response to this 12-mark task: 'A business should locate where wages are lowest.' Consider this view. Set out the paragraphs you would write, the judgement you would reach and the criterion that decides it, the case against your judgement, and the conditions the recommendation would depend on.
items.canonical_answer: Plan. Paragraph 1, terms: locate means the choice of site or country for operations; the view rests its whole case on a single cost figure. Paragraph 2, the case for the view: wages are a large recurring cost for a labour-intensive business, so a lower wage does tend to cut the cost of each unit, and where the work is simple and productivity is similar everywhere, the lowest-wage site can genuinely be the cheapest. Paragraph 3, the case against: the wage is one input among many - transport to the market, materials, taxes, the risk of unfamiliar rules - and output per worker decides the wage cost of a unit as much as the wage does, so the lowest-wage place is often not the lowest-cost place; and for a business that lives on customers reaching it, wages may barely matter at all. Paragraph 4, judgement: the view fails for most businesses most of the time; the criterion that decides it is total cost per unit delivered - and, for customer-facing businesses, access to customers - rather than the wage alone. Paragraph 5, conditions: the recommendation that sets low wages aside holds unless the work is simple, productivity is equal and transport is trivial, in which case the low-wage site wins.

Counterargument: the plan must include the case for the view - labour-intensive work with equal productivity.
Condition: the plan must state the conditions under which the low-wage site would win.

items.prompt: Dragonfly Drones repairs crop-surveying drones for commercial farms. It began in the owner garage; farms now send drones in from three regions. The owner has shortlisted two premises. Site A: a unit in an industrial park with easy lorry access, rent N$5 200 a month, but the park zoning plan lists 'light industrial' uses and the council would need convincing that repair counts. Site B: a shopfront on the main road through town, rent N$8 900 a month, where farmers dropping off drones could combine trips with buying supplies. Analyse the situation and recommend which site Dragonfly Drones should take.
items.canonical_answer: Analysis: the business straddles two location logics. As a workshop it receives and returns equipment, which favours Site A lorry access and lower rent; as a repair service for visiting farmers it lives on customers reaching it, which favours Site B main-road shopfront, and the rent gap of N$3 700 a month is what access to passing farm traffic would cost. The legal dimension at Site A is not a detail: whether repair counts as light industrial under the zoning plan decides whether the site is available at all, and the need to convince the council means delay and a genuine chance of refusal, so the business should investigate the plan before relying on that site; Site B carries no such uncertainty, though its rent bites harder. Recommendation: Site B, provided the business can carry the N$8 900 rent while it grows, because the shopfront removes the zoning risk and puts the service where its customers already travel; the criterion is fit with how this business earns - farmers bringing drones in - not rent alone. The counterargument: Site A N$3 700 monthly saving is material for a young business, and if most drones arrive by courier rather than with the farmer, the passing-trade advantage fades and the industrial site wins. The condition: the recommendation holds if walk-in and drop-off trade drives revenue; if couriered repairs dominate, Site A, with its zoning question answered first, becomes the better choice.
marking_guidance: Judgement: award a clear recommendation between the two sites.
Context: award for using the facts of the business - lorry access, the two rents, the zoning plan light-industrial wording, farmers combining trips.
Criterion: award for naming what decides it: fit with how the business earns, and the zoning risk.
Counterargument: award for the case against: the monthly saving at Site A and couriered repairs.
Condition: award for the recommendation depending on how repairs arrive and the zoning question being answered.
